title: ‘All About Corinne’ Review: Isabelle Huppert Stalks Sandrine Kiberlain in a Witty, Deliciously Acted French Industry Satire
description: As one of the select few French actresses who has earned definite-article status in her homeland — referred to routinely as La Huppert, alongside t
body:
As one of the select few French actresses who has earned definite-article status in her homeland — referred to routinely as La Huppert, alongside the likes of La Binoche and La Deneuve — it’s immediately, amusingly jarring to see Isabelle Huppert cast as a thoroughly indefinite article: a jobbing movie extra whose name nobody recalls, no matter how many headshots and résumés she desperately forces into the hands of higher-ups on set. Casting Huppert as an industry nobody is the chief gag of “All About Corinne,” Marc Fitoussi‘s winningly droll film-biz comedy, but there turns out to be a lot of mileage in it, particularly with co-star Sandrine Kiberlain — cast not just as an industry somebody, but as Sandrine Kiberlain herself — as her imperious foil.
	

	Both sending themselves up in contrasting ways, the stars’ perceptive, vanity-free performances lend some weight and feeling to what is otherwise a frothy exercise — as is to be expected from Fitoussi, a specialist in female-driven French divertissements, including the uncharacteristically chipper Huppert vehicle “Copacabana” and the recent Laure Calamy hit “Two Tickets to Greece.” Given its starry, easy-breezy charms and accessibly inside-baseball humor, “All About Corinne” should have little trouble securing global arthouse distribution following a festival run that began as Locarno’s closing night selection, continuing through gala slots in Toronto and Busan; audiences au fait with “Call Your Agent!” and its good-humored brand of industry satire will feel right at home.


	“You might want to ask yourself why you’re still in the same place at your age,” says a colleague, with casual cruelty, to Corinne Maclou (Huppert), an actress who, for decades, has been steadily and invisibly working at the least glamorous end of the business — and who, in her sixties, hasn’t yet given up hope of stardom. In fringe theater, at least, she’s had the odd inspired moment in the spotlight; in film, she’s lumped with countless other, younger extras and bit players, fighting for the rare gift of a single line. 
	

	Not for lack of ability — Huppert may dim her light a bit, but doesn’t stretch so far as to play a bad actor — she’s simply never had the break, and while Corinne’s efforts to ingratiate herself with A-listers are played for squirm-inducing comedy, there’s also gentle pathos to her desperation, underlined by the ironic star casting. She knows, and we know, that she’s a Huppert-level talent. Why can no one else see it?

	Corinne’s standard line to try curry favor with bigger-name actresses is to cheerfully remark on their physical resemblance to each other, noting that they could play sisters — an approach that doesn’t get the diminutive redhead far with the tall, beachy-haired Kiberlain when they share a scene (or at least occupy the same frame) together. But Corinne’s persistence coincides with a sudden phase of insecurity for the soignée leading lady, who’s trying to cultivate a more down-to-earth image after her agent pithily tells her that “even Cotillard is less detached from reality.” And so she pityingly takes Corinne’s CV, as well as the proferred recording of an obscure Chilean play which Corinne believes to be her finest hour.

	Nothing comes of it, of course, until months later, when Corinne sees the news that Kiberlain is taking to the Paris stage in a production of the very same play, and bitterly confronts her outside the theater. Out of resentment and shamefaced guilt, a highly conditional friendship is forged, as each actress uses the other to very different ends: In Kiberlain, Corinne sees her long-awaited connection to the top; through Corinne, Kiberlain believes she can keep it real. Fitoussi’s writing is fizzy and lightly bitchy throughout, but it’s the stars, playing freely with their respective screen personae, who make it genuinely funny. In a more obvious iteration of this story, their roles might be swapped: There’s as much inherent comedy in Huppert playing a spiraling, faintly tragic rube as in Kiberlain, best known for her neurotic comic work, revealing the brittle hauteur of her “real” self.

	Other good sports turning up as themselves, to wickedly unflattering effect, include Emmanuelle Bercot, tetchily directing a big-budget period drama that could turn things around for Corinne, and Diane Kruger — hilariously glamazonian as she competes with Kiberlain for maximum miscasting in a new Dardenne Brothers film about a tiler in Liège. If that raises a chuckle from you, as it certainly did from this critic, then consider yourself squarely in the film’s target audience. You can cut precisely without cutting too deep: More sweet than scathing, “All About Corinne” loves its stars too much to really draw blood. We love them too, so that’s just fine.

title: Kelly Clarkson vs. Art of Play: Footage Revealed of Singer’s Visit to Brooklyn Novelty Store She Slammed for ‘Pretty Woman’ Treatment
description: Footage of Kelly Clarkson visiting the Brooklyn novelty store she slammed on Saturday has now been acquired and released by Pablo Torre, the host a
body:
Footage of Kelly Clarkson visiting the Brooklyn novelty store she slammed on Saturday has now been acquired and released by Pablo Torre, the host and executive editor of the investigative podcast, “Pablo Torre Finds Out.”

	The video offers another perspective to the ongoing drama between Clarkson and Art of Play, the Brooklyn local business she alleged gave her the “Pretty Woman” treatment when an employee looked at the singer as though she “couldn’t afford” Molly, the $15,000 bird automaton she inquired about purchasing. “Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale,” Clarkson wrote on X before naming the store.
	

	Clarkson can be seen wearing a baseball hat, bright yellow T-shirt, baggy jeans and a backpack in the video. She enters the store, accompanied by her children, and browses and picks up a few items as more shoppers continue to enter. From footage from an alternative camera angle, we can see Clarkson then find herself standing in front of the automaton bird, where she then gets the attention of a store employee, who can be seen speaking with the musician and pointing at something by the bird, though it is not clear from the video what he was pointing at.


	After Art of Play shared a statement in response on Sunday, writing that the bird is “permanently attached to the wall and isn’t for sale” and “plays an important role in the magic shows we host here,” a skeptical Clarkson responded once again, describing the interaction now seen on video and writing: “Cool, cool. Sure, it wasn’t for sale. That’s the narrative Art of Play is gonna go with 👍 so the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn’t happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone ‘yes, it’s for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you I can.’”
	

	At this point in the footage, Clarkson and the employee part ways as he begins helping other customers in the store. Clarkson then puts back the items she was holding, but before she leaves, she turns around and speaks to another employee behind the counter, gesticulating, seemingly upset about the earlier interaction. Other shoppers in the store can be seen looking back at Clarkson, whose entire visit to the store lasted less than five minutes. Her first tweet about the interaction was posted 15 minutes after she left.

	While some are staunchly pro-Clarkson in the debate that has since taken over the internet, others have questioned the singer’s motives for calling out the small business across her social media accounts. In an interview with Inside Edition on Tuesday, store owner Adam Rubin said that his store has been review-bombed since Clarkson took to social media and named the store, and employees and surrounding businesses have been harassed. “We are afraid for the safety of our shopkeepers. Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger… Things changed when she used her platform to attack us. It’s just social warfare,” he said. Rubin also offered an explanation for why Clarkson might have felt she received subpar treatment: “When Kelly came in, the shop was crowded. She was dressed like everybody else in the shop. We treated her like a normal person, but apparently that did not live up to her expectations.” 

	Art of Play is described as a specialty curiosity shop and online retailer.

	Watch the full footage here.

title: ‘Clean Hands’ Review: Zach Braff Is a Cop on a Crusade to Save His Addict Daughter in an Uneasy Fact-Based Crime Drama
description: When a filmmaker tells a story based on real events, especially ones that are inspiring or heroic, there’s always a risk of hagiography. “Clean Han
body:
When a filmmaker tells a story based on real events, especially ones that are inspiring or heroic, there’s always a risk of hagiography. “Clean Hands” is a movie where the storytellers either take a lot of license with an actual person’s life to add drama, or don’t seem aware just how unflattering their subject’s behavior actually is. Written, produced and directed by Jake Allyn (“Ride”), the film chronicles the relationship between real-life Hagerstown, MD narcotics officer Kevin Simmers (Zach Braff) and his efforts to rescue his daughter Brooke (Esther McGregor) from the grip of drug abuse. But while the “happening right under his nose” details lend a heartbreaking edge to a sadly familiar story, the script’s argument against criminalizing addiction reconciles uneasily with its portrayal of Simmers’ determination to save Brooke by any means necessary.
	

	Simmers is a hero cop, looked up to by his colleagues and liked better than one might expect by the local townspeople, given his by-the-book approach. Though he maintains a close relationship with 19-year-old Brooke, he’s blindsided when he learns that she’s addicted to Percocet and has been consorting with abusive dealer Brick (Kraig Dane). After unsuccessfully trying to enroll her in a private rehab facility, Simmers learns that she’s moved on to heroin; he takes a tough-love approach to let her get arrested, hoping to scare her straight. But when even that fails, he becomes determined to cut off her supply at the source, pursuing local addicts in the hopes of apprehending anyone who might deal her drugs.
	

	Despite the support of his religious wife Dana (Abigail Spencer) and colleagues on the police force, including an ambitious deputy (Lucas Till) eager to succeed him as the precinct’s role model, Simmers’ efforts to help get Brooke clean fail over and over again. As he faces the prospect of losing her to addiction, he begins to conceive an alternative path for struggling drug abusers, even while witnessing members of the Hagerstown community — including some of his fellow officers — exploiting addicts instead of helping them.

	Given the infomercial pasted at the top of the closing credits for Brooke’s House, the rehab facility Simmers created in response to his daughter’s addiction, it feels safe to assume that the former police officer fully endorsed this portrait of him and his family’s struggles. Yet the typical disclaimer absolving the filmmakers of responsibility for dramatizing these real people’s lives is oddly posted at the beginning of the closing credits rather than at the very end, suggesting that some of the narrative leaps taken here by the filmmakers are bigger than usual. To that end, one can understand why Allyn wouldn’t want to risk misrepresenting Hagerstown law enforcement. But should audiences accept at face value every action taken by Simmers in his crusade to save his daughter?

	By all accounts, he was a dedicated cop with honed instincts as an investigator, and a loving father to Brooke — so much so that, in the film, Dana accuses the two of them of being addicted to each other. But the character’s compassion towards perpetrators and his cool detachment under pressure seem only to apply when he doesn’t have an active stake in a crime. When he does, he seems willing to abuse his power and take any measures that he thinks will result in whatever he’s already decided the outcome should be — whether that’s lying to a healthcare provider to get his daughter treatment, or arresting an individual he deems complicit in Brooke’s condition. 

	As the film tells it, Simmers eventually learns that waging war against dealers and community enablers makes less of an impact on people who are addicted than providing them consistent, patient, loving support. But the character is so relentless for so long with his methods that it’s hard not to pin a portion of the blame for Brooke’s addiction on him.
	

	Again, that seems distantly like the point (or at least one point) of “Clean Hands.” But Allyn is entirely too interested in Simmers’ police work, meaning high-pitched chases and strong-arm interrogations, to strike the right balance between his day job and his earnest efforts to help his daughter. As a viewer, it’s possible to forgive a character who’s so determined to protect his daughter that he takes overbearing or inappropriate measures, but when the film wants the crime stuff to be tense and exciting — amplified with music by instrumental rock act Those Who Ride With Giants — it undercuts the humanity of what that character is facing.

	Simmers marks a departure from the kinds of roles for which Braff is best known, and the actor commits to the character’s tenacity and determination in a way that suggests he’s either prioritizing authenticity regardless of how the character is perceived, or he misunderstands how sympathetic Allyn’s version of Simmers can be. The problem is the contrast between his well-meaning actions and their impact on others: Brooke faces beatings in jail because her father antagonizes the guards and other inmates, God-fearing Dana flinches every time he drops an f-bomb or angrily dresses down a rehab administrator, and until the very last scene in the film, he ignores or dismisses the addiction, poverty or desperation of anyone he encounters who’s struggling.

	McGregor offers a welcome counterbalance as Brooke, whose general disposition emanates from her relationship with her father, even as it’s hobbled by troubles the script pinpoints with delicacy. Though the film doesn’t quite know what to do with Dana as Simmers bulldozes his way to a cure for Brooke, Spencer similarly offers grace — or at least a less rigid form of support — that hints at how his initial way of helping may not be the most effective one.

	To whatever extent this story is told accurately, Simmers was of course doing the best that he could to reckon with a challenge he’d dealt with in the line of duty, but never with a person so close to him — and years of repetition reinforced a one-size-fits-all reaction to an affliction that must be addressed individually. But the film builds to the founding of Brooke’s House and its immediate, overwhelming success, indicating that all Simmers needed to do was change his tactics, instead of the more meaningful, moving change in his perception of addiction as something to be mechanically repaired. A handful of appealing performances aside, “Clean Hands” ignores too many messy realities in favor of quick solutions; the stuff that gives a true story like this power is the hard work and struggle that happens between an epiphany about oneself and the reality of implementing its lessons in the world.

title: Stephen Amell Says Putting on the ‘Baywatch’ Red Trunks Felt ‘So Familiar’ Because ‘It’s a Superhero Show’
description: Stephen Amell, star of the upcoming “Baywatch” reboot, first came to public attention as Oliver Queen in DC superhero series “Arrow.” But the actor
body:
Stephen Amell, star of the upcoming “Baywatch” reboot, first came to public attention as Oliver Queen in DC superhero series “Arrow.” But the actor says his new role isn’t so different.

	“Once I got on it and I put on the red trunks, I realized, like, why does this feel so familiar?” Amell said of working on “Baywatch.” “It’s because it’s a superhero show. That’s what it feels like to me, and that makes my job easy.”
	

	While spending the working day on the beach might seem like a dream job, Amell went on to explain the reality was somewhat different. “I thought that when I was doing ‘Arrow,’ that shooting from 7 o’clock at night until 7 o’clock in the morning on a rooftop or in a damp building somewhere in Vancouver was going to be the toughest thing that I ever did,” the actor revealed during a panel at Mipcom in Cannes, France. “But man, sunrise to sunset on the beach in Venice, you go through all of the emotions. At some point you’re hot. At some point you’re cold. At some point you’re probably itchy. It was a lot.”




	

					Stephen Amell and Brooks Nader attend the “Baywatch” photocall during MIPCOM 2026 at the Palais des Festivals (courtesy of Mipcom)
									Frederic DIDES/360 medias
	



	He added: “But man, getting to shoot, especially on Venice Beach — my family and I rented a house there – like, this is the California dream and adventure. It was so special.”

	“Baywatch” first launched in 1989. The show, which is owned by Fremantle, ran for 11 seasons and at its peak was one of the world’s most-watched show with over a billion viewers every week across 200 countries, turning its cast – including David Hasselhoff and Pamela Anderson – into superstars.
	

	The 12-episode reboot, which is produced by Fremantle and Fox Entertainment, sees a new cast of lifeguards don the red bathing suits including Amell, Brooks Nader and Shay Mitchell. Some original cast members are also set to make an appearance, with David Chokachi reprising the role of Cody Madison while Erika Eleniak, Michael Bergin and Kelly Packard return as guest stars.

	Fox president Michael Thorne, who joined Amell on the Mipcom panel alongside Nader and Fremantle CEO Jens Richter, said it was important to the team to “embrace what made the show so special: heroism, escapism, a beautiful, intelligent, heroic, flawed cast of characters” while at the same time updating the series for a modern audience.

	“The original rescues are so funny,” he acknowledged. “Pamela Anderson would walk up to the edge of the beach, she wouldn’t even put her feet in the water — her hair was perfect, her makeup was on — and she’d reach out very gently and be like, ‘Okay, I saved you!’ And that just doesn’t do it [for viewers today].”

	“So we tried to capture the heart and the humanity, the juicy soap, and I think where we really elevated it is in the rescues and what it means to be a lifeguard today.”

	“Baywatch” bows in Jan. 2027 on Fox. Fox Entertainment Global holds domestic distribution rights while Fremantle is repping global sales.

title: Why the ‘Girls’ Revival Is Such an Exciting Idea
description: The return of “Girls” for a five-episode limited run won’t just be interesting because of how Hannah Horvath has or has not changed. It’ll be a lit
body:
The return of “Girls” for a five-episode limited run won’t just be interesting because of how Hannah Horvath has or has not changed. It’ll be a litmus test for how we at home have, as well.

	After all, Lena Dunham has at times struggled to distinguish herself from her most famous creation. At the height of HBO’s “Girls,” the op-ed-generating machine that, incidentally, was a very good TV show, journalists wrote about and addressed Dunham as if she literally were the narcissistic writer she portrayed onscreen. A general consensus seemed to have formed that Dunham could not possibly understand the ways in which Horvath was flawed and annoying — despite the fact that Dunham had written her. And, in the years after “Girls” wrapped up in 2017, Dunham struggled to step out of the show’s shadow with new work, in part due to medical and substance issues she documented in her recent memoir “Famesick.”
	

	As proven by “Famesick” and her 2025 Netflix series “Too Much” — a wistful, surprisingly mature story of attempting to move on from romantic disappointment — Dunham is in a different place now, and so, maybe, is her audience. Her book was received with warm nostalgia and appreciation for Dunham’s lacerating understanding of herself and the web of misunderstandings that surround her.


	So — while it’s obviously too early even to speculate about what a late-2020s “Girls” might look like, aside from its cast, with Dunham, Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet and Andrew Rannells confirmed to return — there’s hope that it might cut through some of the clutter that came to define the show as it ran on. It’s also reasonable to assume that “Girls” 2 might more fully reflect Dunham’s perspective than did the show we now remember fondly: Part of the tension and drama of “Famesick” is its depiction of “Girls” as the product of a vexed series of compromises with Dunham’s then-creative partner Jenni Konner, brought in to teach the raw writing-directing talent behind the indie film “Tiny Furniture” how to make conventionally structured TV. Judd Apatow returns to this iteration “Girls” as an executive producer, but Konner does not.
	

	The Dunham-Konner breakup — Dunham’s side of which is painstakingly reconstructed in “Famesick” — lends the idea of a “Girls” revival an intriguingly meta aspect. Wherever Hannah is now, she’ll likely be written by a person newly working on her own terms. (Along with co-writers, Dunham is credited as a writer on every episode of “Too Much,” which was not true of the first six seasons of “Girls.”) And the information Dunham has shared about her inner life lends the revival the feeling of a reclamation, as well. Hannah’s ending on the series — isolated from many of her friends and raising a child as a single mother — was, we now know, written at a time when Dunham was physically ill and addicted to drugs. Making the series in what seems to be a happier and stabler moment in her life — including with a new perspective on parenthood, as Dunham, having written about her grief following her hysterectomy, is now a mother — allows the possibility of Hannah finding a deeper, richer ending.

	Or… not an ending, but a stopping point. As this news proves once again, nothing in TV is ever really final — does anyone believe, for instance, that we’ll actually never see Carrie Bradshaw again? But the Carrie example gives a sense of the potential, and pitfalls, of a “Girls” revival. It was joyful and heartening for fans of that show to check in with Carrie and her friends on the streets of New York in the 2008 sequel film and 2020s HBO Max revival “And Just Like That.” (I use “streets of New York” advisedly — note that I am avoiding mentioning the words “Abu Dhabi.”) And these new projects allowed Michael Patrick King to test out how the characters of “Sex and the City” might move through passages of life as they grew into late middle age — a genuinely radical project. But as “And Just Like That” ran on, Carrie could at times feel less like the living, breathing person she once had and more like an accumulation of narrative contrivances — back with Aidan, again! — and opportunities to comment on changing social mores.

	In all, though, it was invigorating to see Carrie Bradshaw ripped out of her moment and placed into contemporaneity. And Hannah Horvath has similar promise. Since “Girls” ended, she’s been frozen in time — our reactions to her may have shifted, but she remains a creature of the late Obama era, as emblematic of old-millennial mores and ways of speaking as Carrie Bradshaw was of turn-of-the-century Gen X fabulosity. How has Hannah’s perspective shifted since we left her — and what parts of her remain irreducibly herself? Much in the same way that I’ve loved watching Dunham coming into herself in recent years, I can’t wait to find out.

schema.headline: Why the ‘Girls’ Revival Is Such an Exciting Idea

title: ‘Just Dance: Decades of Hits’ Costume Designer Breaks Down the New Game’s Look and Not Using AI: ‘It’s Our Art’
description:
At a time when AI is increasingly being used to replace human creativity, “Just Dance” is refusing to change its hands-on approach.

	The Ubisoft d
body:
At a time when AI is increasingly being used to replace human creativity, “Just Dance” is refusing to change its hands-on approach.

	The Ubisoft dance game, which just launched “Just Dance: Decades of Hits” on Tuesday, brings on-screen characters to life through a process rooted in human labor. Real dancers wear handmade costumes, wigs and makeup before being filmed against a green screen and integrated into the game.


	“We are really loving what we do. It’s our art. It’s what we love,” Benjamin Jouffret, the game’s costume designer and character lead, tells Variety. “We are proud of working, sketching ourselves, creating what is in our minds and making real costumes with real costume makers.”
	

	Jouffret says his team is committed to creating its characters without AI. Having studied fashion and previously working as a stylist, Jouffret has spent the past eight years overseeing the costumes and characters that appear on-screen.

	The process begins with a brainstorming session, during which the creative team listens to a song and watches its music video to determine the direction of a character. Sometimes the team draws inspiration directly from the artist, other times opting to take the concept in a completely different direction.



	

					The concept art and finished product for Zara Larsson’s “Midnight Sun” for “Just Dance: Decades of Hits.”
	



	These decisions also inform the game’s maps, which combine the characters with their backgrounds and surrounding environments. “If you want to create a map for the community or the hardcore players, we know that they will really want to have a connection with the singers,” Jouffret explains. “If you have a Lady Gaga song, you want Easter eggs. For that, we are really inspired by the artists.”
	

	From there, the team determines whether the dance will feature a solo performer or a duo or trio, as well as the type of character that fits best. Sometimes, up to 10 characters will be featured in one dance.

	“We also decide if you want a casual costume, or an alien or a mascot or a nonbinary character,” Joufrett says. “We do a lot of things.”

	His team then assembles mood boards using references from films, music videos and other media before developing sketches and finalizing designs. Once a concept is approved, the team consults its roster of dancers to find someone who can embody the character and complement the choreographer’s vision.

	Overall, the timeline is relatively short. After a one-day brainstorming session, the team typically spends two to three weeks designing a character, followed by roughly four weeks of production. That period includes fittings, hair and makeup tests and rehearsals to ensure the costumes work with the choreography. Filming takes place over a single day.



	

					The sketch and final product of the costume for Bad Bunny’s “Nuevayol” in “Just Dance: Decades of Hits.”
	



	Across the game’s Paris-based lead studio and its partner studio in Shanghai, the team creates roughly 100 costumes per installment, balancing visual appeal with practicality.

	“We can’t make beautiful costumes if they can’t be used by the dancers,” Jouffret explains. “We can do what we want, but we have to do it smartly.”

	The team previously experimented with 3D printing, but the materials proved too heavy for dancers to move comfortably in. Today, that technique is reserved for accessories requiring smaller, intricate details.

	For Jouffret, the trial and error of the process is part of what makes the game so special. “We really love to create and make things by ourselves,” he says.



	

					The sketch for the costume for Billy Joel’s “Uptown Girl” in “Just Dance: Decades of Hits.”
	



	His team collaborates with costume makers and other specialists, each bringing expertise in areas such as mascots, corsets and casual wear. The team’s commitment to representation is also reflected in the game itself, which features dancers with different backgrounds and abilities. In one installment, the team worked with dancer Jana Bruno, who has one arm, earning recognition for its diversity efforts.
	

	“Just Dance” releases a new installment every year, sometimes revisiting characters and storylines from previous games. For “Decades of Hits,” one new character, Lyra, is the daughter of a character introduced in a previous game. Players will follow her storyline of searching for her father through dance.

	Meanwhile, hundreds of costumes from the franchise’s 17-year history remain in storage in Paris, forming a physical archive of the work behind the game’s characters. Jouffret says the team hopes to showcase the creations through a potential exhibition or runway presentation, although some pieces would need repairs after the wear and tear of filming.

title: ‘Once Upon in the Middle East’ Review: China’s Oscar Entry Is a Breakneck Blockbuster That Mixes Food Porn With Wartime Devastation
description:
Oct 13, 2026 3:21pm PT	
	

	
		‘Once Upon in the Middle East’ Review: China’s Oscar Entry Is a Breakneck Blockbuster That Mixes Food
body:
Oct 13, 2026 3:21pm PT	
	

	
		‘Once Upon in the Middle East’ Review: China’s Oscar Entry Is a Breakneck Blockbuster That Mixes Food Porn With Wartime Devastation
	

	Bafflingly entertaining and politically reprehensible, this antiwar epic follows a Chinese chef through a whirlwind of absurd and brutal events at the outbreak of the Iraq War.
	
			


			
			
	

									Dirty Monkeys
	

		
	
				

	Not since Zhang Yimou’s 2002 wuxia spectacle “Hero” has China landed an Oscar nomination for Best International Feature — and this dry spell surely won’t be broken with this year’s bombastic submission “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” Like most of the country’s entries over the past decade, this blockbuster epic — a summer box office hit at home — makes for an extravagant display of the strength of the nation’s commercial film industry. Strength, in the sense that no modest operation could conceivably pull off the technical wizardry and large-scale worldbuilding showcased here, where an entire city is at one point turned into an inferno of crumbling buildings, and a massive military base is, in a later scene, ambushed in a rain of blazing pyrotechnics.
	

	The film is also, as expected from this state-backed production, blatantly propagandistic — but in a way that is particularly baffling, and shockingly tasteless. If those sound like the elements for a good time, in the B-movie sense, then you are also correct. Against the odds, “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” is also, both regrettably and miraculously, extremely watchable. The Jekyll part of your brain will tell you to leave but the Hyde-side will keep you seated in morbid, twitchy-eyed fascination over the film’s two-and-a-half hour runtime.


	To cut straight to the point, this is a film in which China symbolically emerges from the rubble of the Iraq War as a pacifistic patriarch and guardian of all the world’s children. Director Wen Muyue delivers this subtext through the story of Xu Fu (Shen Teng), a debt-ridden chef who agrees to temporarily take over a Chinese restaurant in the fictional Gulf-region city of Bahata, intending to return to his daughter and mother in China in two years time. 
	

	Flash-forwards to an elder Xu Fu with liver spots and a conspicuous scar on his cheek tell us that he will indeed make it back to his family, but it’ll take much longer than a few years — the frankly absurd reasons for his delay a consequence of his, let’s say, geopolitical misfortunes. He’s a man in the wrong place at the wrong time, though, cleverly, the film makes the point that a good Chinese meal is never unwelcome. In fact it’s globally in demand — a lifeline that ensures Xu Fu’s survival through the film’s whirlwind of events.

	Before we get to the grisly images of dead children covered in ash, the film starts out as a feel-good dramedy in which Xu Fu adapts to his new surroundings. Frazzled softie Ma Junsheng (Jiang Qiming), the restaurant manager, is our hero’s bridge between China and his new home, translating for Xu Fu between Arabic and Chinese during tense but diplomatic discussions with the restaurant owner Zaid (Sherif Sabby). Glossy, mouthwatering closeups of grilled meats and bubbling stone-pot stews testify to the success of Xu Fu’s kitchen takeover. Nurturing local talent is also on the agenda when he takes on a mentee, Seif (Omar Sharif — no, not that one), an angsty orphan who learns to sublimate his rage into the art of Chinese cooking. Though as the film goes on, this anger grows into a furious, war-hardened desire for retribution. Does a delicious roasted duck stand a chance? It does, in this film’s mind, with the help of the preternaturally compassionate Xu Fu.

	“Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” is something of a both-sides film in that both the Americans and the not-so-thinly-veiled Iraqis are gross caricatures of themselves, and there’s particular ire reserved for that most treacherous of abominations: Chinese-American … food. In epic-handshake-meme solidarity, Xu Fu and Zaid agree that their restaurant will never serve U.S.-style Chinese dishes like General Tso’s chicken; and when the US troops bomb Bahata to smithereens and occupy the city, a crass Chinese-American private (Aarif Lee Zhi-ting) bullies his way into free meals at Xu Fu’s restaurant. Not a pushover but a practical-minded realist, the chef takes the punches, striking up a booze-smuggling deal with the Americans to keep the orphans living in his restaurant safe.
	

	The maddening implausibility that sustains the film’s relentless, weirdly hypnotizing forward momentum means we’re never in one place — or one mood — for too long. Zaid’s home is bombed in one intensely melodramatic sequence that culminates in a slow zoom over Zaid cradling his dead wife and child. Next thing we know, he’s radicalized and joins a terrorist group. Xu Fu, Ma Junsheng and Seif — the cooking trio — are promptly captured by the U.S. Army and forced to preside over the kitchen on base. This allows for more sumptuous shots of delicious food while Xu Fu is, for whatever reason, targeted by an aggro, block-jawed American soldier. Xu Fu and Ma Junsheng also play surrogate dads to Seif, whose increasingly violent eruptions threaten to change the course of his life more than once.

	For all its dewy-eyed sentimentality, the film is also startlingly brutal and bloody, making for a deranged whiplash effect that’s felt most powerfully in the film’s final act, which is set in a terrorist stronghold where pipsqueaks are brainwashed into becoming suicide bombers. Cozy, brotherly scenes (as when Ma Junsheng slips Seif a smuggled can of soda) are directly followed by executions and montages of plush-bear-wielding kiddies invoking jihad. There’s a slickness to the carnage that rubs uncomfortably against the film’s humanist ethos, rendering artificial (for all Shen Teng’s trembling and mouth-contorting labors) the horrific tragedies that befall its characters. It’s a vision of wartime brutality that’s both blithely matter-of-fact and desperate to pull at our heartstrings; utterly delusional, in other words, and hard to look away from.


	
		More from Variety

schema.headline: ‘Once Upon in the Middle East’ Review: China’s Oscar Entry Is a Breakneck Blockbuster That Mixes Food Porn With Wartime Devastation

title: ‘Tommy & Tuppence’ Stars Josh Dylan and Antonia Thomas on That ‘Intense’ Finale, Why the Detective Duo ‘Keep Missing Each Other’ Romantically and a Potential Season 2
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for Episode 6 of “Tommy & Tuppence,” now streaming on BritBox. 

	The finale of “Tommy & Tuppence” find
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for Episode 6 of “Tommy & Tuppence,” now streaming on BritBox. 

	The finale of “Tommy & Tuppence” finds the Agatha Christie detective duo, played by Josh Dylan and Antonia Thomas, on the verge of a new chapter.

	The BritBox Original series brings the classic characters into the modern day, where Tommy and Tuppence are exes instead of a married couple (as Christie originally wrote). A decade after dating at university, they bump into each other at a wedding and soon become embroiled in a murder mystery. The two have an exciting will they-won’t they chemistry as they solve cases around London (with the help of Tommy’s Aunt Ada, played by Imelda Staunton), begin their own private detective business and start getting closer. But there’s just one problem — Tuppence is married to a director back in L.A. 
	

	The series’ sixth episode sees Tommy and Tuppence solve a cold case surrounding harrowing child murders in the countryside, just as Tuppence at last acknowledges her feelings for Tommy and decides to divorce her husband. In classic rom-com fashion, just as Tuppence bursts through Tommy’s door with the news, she sees him kissing police detective Draper (Callie Cooke). Then, Tuppence’s sister presents them with their biggest mission yet: helping the U.K. government with a major case. 


	“Finally, it clicks and she realizes — but is she just a bit too late?” Thomas tells Variety over Zoom.  

	“Much of their relationship is characterized by sliding doors moments and missing each other just by a hair’s breath, which is in part infuriating but also kind of tantalizing,” Dylan adds. “It’s like, when are they going to get it out?!” 
	

	Below, Dylan and Thomas break down the finale episode, reveal how they established Tommy and Tuppence’s chemistry and discuss a potential Season 2.
	
		First of all, what made you want to come on board the series?	

	Dylan: Obviously, Agatha Christie is untouchable in so many ways — incomparable rather, because she’s the Queen of Crime and it’s beloved by people. But when I read the scripts I felt like, here’s an opportunity to do something that I don’t think I’ve seen before, which is blending that cozy crime world, that Agatha Christie world, with an opportunity to make this feel really grounded and naturalistic and real. 

	Thomas: Tommy and Tuppence are amateurs anyway, so it lends itself really well to the more modern-day idea of being a sleuth and listening to a podcast and trying to figure something out yourself. Like we can all relate to that; I love a true crime podcast. And the way that [Christie] wrote those characters was quite modern actually, for the time. Particularly Tuppence being a pretty outspoken, front-footed woman, she was very modern in the way that she behaved. So that felt like a very easy transfer.
	
		Tommy and Tuppence are married in Christie’s stories, but in this adaptation they’re exes in this sort of will they-won’t they phase. How did you establish that chemistry?	

	Thomas: Josh and I did a lot of meeting up and trying to work on the relationship and find a colloquial shorthand in and amongst the text. I certainly was quite daunted by the scenes where there’s quite a lot of exposition and they’re going through and trying to figure out the crime. I remember being like, “I don’t know how to do this!” And Josh was like, “I think these are the moments that they’re having the most fun and also when they as characters are connecting the most.” And as soon as you said that, it totally unlocked it for me. Because there’s two things going on, which is really fun about Tommy and Tuppence — the relationship between them and the crimes that they’re solving. So to use the crime-solving as a way to become closer was so fun. And then [writer] Phoebe [Eclair-Powell] was really open with allowing us to be freer with some of those bits to make it feel more modern.

	Dylan: Yeah, and moments where it allowed for a little bit of improvisation. They let us get away with some of that, which was kind of them. 
	



	

					Antonia Thomas and Josh Dylan in “Tommy & Tuppence.”
									Lara Cornell/LOOKOUT POINT / BRI
	


	
		What were the conversations you had about Tommy and Tuppence’s history? 	

	Dylan: We’re still piecing bits together, to be honest. I think the idea is that they met at university and were together and obviously had an amazing connection, but the details, the reason why they split up is still a bit contentious. They get along and they have this care for each other, but you grow up a lot in 10 years. So at the top of the series and throughout, you’re seeing these people that have this core chemistry and connection, but they’re realizing the ways in which they’ve changed and the ways they’re still the same. And that feels really human and real and truthful to me, and was really interesting to play.Thomas: And also, as much as they have changed, they’re still the same. It’s like that idea of a leopard doesn’t change its spots. The thing that was the problem last time, 10 years ago, is still basically the problem. It’s just, are they more mature? Can they address things differently?Dylan: But on the flip side, the spark that drew them together in the first place is also still there, in exactly the same way.
	
		What makes them work so well together in a more professional sense, as a detective duo?	

	Thomas: I think the fact that they’re quite opposites. They’re the yin and yang, they complement each other. Tuppence is pretty impulsive, she’s very instinctual and has often a strong gut feeling about things and is quite ballsy. So she’ll want to attack things head on, and then Tommy is much more thoughtful and precise and forensic often about things, which is really needed. The push and pull between them I think keeps them steady and in the middle.
	
		And I have to ask, what was it like working with Imelda Staunton as Aunt Ada?	

	Dylan: What a legend. She’s cool as hell and very twinkly and magical. And seems to kind of be the perfect Aunt Ada.Thomas: There’s so much fun to her, like she brought such a fun, almost impish, brilliant side to Ada. And working with her and just watching her work, she’s such a seasoned veteran. It was a brilliant.
	
		Let’s get into the final episode. It’s quite intense — you’re hunting down Jane Lancaster, a child murderer who then sets the house you’re all in on fire, and then Tuppence finally confesses her feelings to Tommy while he’s unconscious. What was that like to film?	

	Dylan: Oh my god, that’s actually a bit triggering. I just got flashbacks to being in that cottage and being in the room with the wonderful actress Alice Krige as Jane Lancaster — being in this tiny little bedroom with her for like, two days. It was so intense.

	Thomas: You had to do your big ol’ speech, didn’t you?

	Dylan: Absolutely glorious monologue. And then being carried out of the fire, I remember Antonia — she’s an incredible actress anyway, full stop the end, but I remember this particular take where I was a dead weight on the floor like, succumbed to the flames, and she was over my face and then a tear fell in my mouth.

	Thomas: [Laughs] And then we were also really tired because that was the end of the shoot. I don’t know if I’ve done a job as intense because we’re basically in every scene, bar a few. And so by the time we got to Episodes 5 and 6, we’d been going for a few months. And then those two episodes just ramped up and it’s just really dark, isn’t it? It’s about child murder and kidnapping and Ada dies and that’s really sad. And then between the two of them as well, they’re not in a good place. 
	



	

					Josh Dylan and Antonia Thomas in “Tommy & Tuppence.”
									Lara Cornell/LOOKOUT POINT / BRI
	


	
		Do you think Tommy heard Tuppence’s confession? At the end, he seems to be moving on with Draper…	

	Thomas: No, I don’t think he does. I think that’s what’s sort of sad about it, in a way. And about the ending altogether. Finally, it clicks and she realizes — but is she just a bit too late? Dylan: Much of their relationship is characterized by sliding doors moments and kind of missing each other just by a hair’s breath, which is in part infuriating but also kind of tantalizing. And they’re not always the best — shock, horror – at expressing themselves. They clearly feel a huge amount, they’re very sensitive and very compassionate and feeling, but they just keep missing each other. It’s like, when are they going to get it out?!
	
		It’s almost like we need a second season! And the ending sets that up quite well, with an offer for the duo to help the government on a case. What would you want to see from a potential Season 2?	

	Thomas: Would love a second season.Dylan: I would love to do one.Thomas: Also, can we do it somewhere exotic?Dylan: Yeah, the Caribbean? We’ll take Spain! No, to be fair, we’d love to do it. These characters have so much scope and potential and range to go on so many more adventures, and we love the creative team. It does feel like Season 1 ends at a very exciting junction, and they grow a lot as well. What I love about this show is that it’s grounded and funny and doesn’t take itself too seriously a lot of the time, but then I do think it has the capacity in moments to go to some darker places and stretch. So I think that would be quite nice, to continue that theme.

	This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity.

schema.headline: ‘Tommy & Tuppence’ Stars Josh Dylan and Antonia Thomas on That ‘Intense’ Finale, Why the Detective Duo ‘Keep Missing Each Other’ Romantically and a Potential Season 2

title: Drake Bell Blasts SAG-AFTRA After Losing Health Insurance: ‘Do Not Become an Actor. Do Not Join SAG’
description:
“Drake & Josh” actor Drake Bell is putting SAG-AFTRA on blast after he revealed he does not qualify for health insurance.

	On his Instagram Story
body:
“Drake & Josh” actor Drake Bell is putting SAG-AFTRA on blast after he revealed he does not qualify for health insurance.

	On his Instagram Story on Tuesday, Bell posted a screenshot of the SAG-AFTRA health plan website that says “you do not qualify for Health Plan coverage at this time. Your reported covered earnings from July 2025-June 2026 did not meet minimum eligibility requirements, or you did not qualify other eligibility rules.”
	

	The webpage says that Bell has earned $17,480.53 and that he needs $11,452.47 more to qualify by reaching the $28,933 required for the SAG-AFTRA Health Plan.


	“Do not become an actor. Do not join SAG. You can work for 35 years and they still say [middle finger emoji],” Bell wrote on the screenshot. He then tagged SAG-AFTRA and its president, “Lord of the Rings” and “The Goonies” actor Sean Astin, in his scathing message.

	“@SAGAFTRA really though @SeanAstin you’re doing a bang up job. How about stop using actors to run things maybe? They literally just know how to say words in front of a camera.”

	Bell has recently turned to music and voice work after his acting career slowed down following Nickelodeon’s “Drake & Josh” series in the 2000s. In 2024, he came forward on the docuseries “Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV” and revealed that he’d been sexually abused as a teen by dialogue coach Brian Peck.

	Bell is the latest celebrity to speak out about troubles obtaining SAG-AFTRA health insurance. “Atypical” actor Jack Haven and “Princess Diaries” star Heather Matarazzo both revealed last month that they wouldn’t qualify for health insurance if they didn’t get more work soon.
	

	“I’m in a bit of an emergency situation,” Haven said in a YouTube video at the time. “I need to make $4,000 by the end of the month in order to qualify for SAG health insurance starting in January.” Haven later obtained enough work after reaching out publicly, and Matarazzo shared that she faced a similar situation.

	“I am literally in the same boat right now. Lots of my fellow actors are,” she wrote. “I remember a time when we didn’t have to earn a minimum to qualify for insurance. Glad to see that Jack has gotten an offer that will let them to qualify for 2027.”

	Variety has reached out to representatives for SAG-AFTRA and Bell for further comment.

schema.headline: Drake Bell Blasts SAG-AFTRA After Losing Health Insurance: ‘Do Not Become an Actor. Do Not Join SAG’

title: Chuck Lorre Tells All: His 10 Years in Scientology, Clashes With Stars Like Roseanne and Brett Butler, and How ‘The Big Bang Theory’ Cast Shocked Him
description: Chuck Lorre has been entangled with some of the most notoriously difficult TV comedy stars in modern memory: Roseanne Barr, Brett Butler, Cybill Sh
body:
Chuck Lorre has been entangled with some of the most notoriously difficult TV comedy stars in modern memory: Roseanne Barr, Brett Butler, Cybill Shepherd and, of course, Charlie Sheen. Of the four, he’s only made up with Sheen — and that rift took years to repair, as their “Two and a Half Men” meltdown was perhaps the ugliest clash of all.

	In his new book “Sitcom: A Memoir” — ironically titled, since he hasn’t traditionally been a fan of the term — Lorre recounts the highs and lows of his career. He often names names — many of whom don’t necessarily come off well in the book.
	

	“Roseanne” producer Carsey-Werner is taken to task, as is former CBS boss Leslie Moonves. Lorre shares his befuddlement in the actions of some of his TV show co-creators and admits he was disappointed when the cast of “The Big Bang Theory” wouldn’t take a salary haircut to share the wealth with some of the show’s newer stars.


	Lorre also — half-jokingly, half-not — blames the Writers Guild’s 2007-2008 strike for the death of democracy, noting how the lack of scripted TV product led the networks to rely more on reality series like Donald Trump’s “The Apprentice.”

	But most of Lorre’s barbs are directed at himself. He details his rocky relationship with his mother, his struggles with “alcoholism, soul-crushing poverty, life-threatening illness, decade in a religious cult, three failed marriages, lifetime prescription for Valacyclovir” and bad choices he’s made. That includes signing away the games and home video residuals to the theme song he wrote for “Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.”
	

	“I decided if I’m going to do this, I’m going to tell the truth as best I can,” he says. “There was no point in doing it if I was going to sugarcoat my life.”

	Among his admissions, Lorre’s ten-year journey through Scientology may be the most surprising thing that execs, stars and producers who have worked with Lorre over the years may learn. For the first time, Lorre reveals that as a young, starving musician, he was invited to a Church of Scientology event. Soon, he had signed a Sea Org employment contract for one billion years.

	Lorre spent the next decade as a Scientologist — and he admits that as his dad was dying, “I actually thought I could heal him with Scientology.” Soon after, Lorre contracted severe ulcerative colitis. But as his own illness got worse, Lorre still believed, “no worries, Scientology would heal me.”

	When Lorre and his then-wife, Paula, decided to finally quit the church, they were immediately excommunicated by their Scientology friends. But because Lorre at the time was destitute, the church didn’t make an effort to keep him. “The church is known to chase members who leave, imploring and/or threatening them to return,” he writes. “Turns out this is only true if the departing thetans have any money. We were so broke, no one noticed we were gone.”

	So, why did Lorre never reveal his Scientology past until now? “It was always a great source of embarrassment to me,” he says. “I burned a decade of my life up in that thing. I can wallow in regret, but I’ve chosen to recognize that even that was a step that had to be taken to get to where I am.”



	

	



	Here are a few more things we learned about Lorre from “Sitcom”:


He changed his last name to “Lorre” because he hated “Levine,” which he says his mother used like a curse word. His wife at the time suggested he change it to “Laurie,” keeping the “CL” initials. “I chimed in with the clever idea to spell it fancy, Lorre, completely unaware that it’s the name of a closeted gay English actor or a misspelling of the men’s clothing store my mom worked at when I was a latchkey kid.”
On “Roseanne,” writers would frequently pen scripts — and then have to attach Tom Arnold’s name, as if he had written them. Lorre also recounts required attendance at Arnold’s many sobriety parties and how exec producers Marcy Carsey and Tom Werner were banned from the set. “If ABC execs had a problem with the show, they had to go directly to the star and beg to be heard,” he writes. “I remember seeing Bob Iger, then the president of ABC, unhappily trudging to her dressing room in the hopes of getting the network’s notes addressed. I can’t confirm this, but I was told she liked making him do his while she was getting a massage.”
When “Roseanne” writer Amy Sherman (now Amy Sherman-Palladino) told Lorre, she would never marry, he bet her $10,000 that she would before 30. She did, marrying Daniel Palladino. Years later, he ran into the couple in a valet line and brought up the unpaid bet. “I let Amy off the hook by suggesting she donate the $10,000 to a charity of my choosing,” he writes. “I’m still waiting.”
“Grace Under Fire” was “just a big, heartbreaking nightmare” under star Brett Butler, he writes. “She hated that her romantic interest was Dave Thomas, and insisted she could do better. She hated the scripts. She very quickly decided she hated me. She threw a full can of Coke at one of my writers, barely missing his head. She asked me to give a speaking part to an extra — for reasons left to my imagination. She rubbed up against young PAs who had no choice but to quietly sit and wait it out. To my knowledge, Carsey-Werner did nothing.”
On “Cybill,” Lorre says that in success, star Cybill Shepherd “became a different person. She made her toady manager a co-exec, and angrily demanded complete control of the stories, scripts, casting, cameras, lighting, editing and probably craft services. After every table read and rehearsal, I would be ordered to her trailer, where I had to sit on a footstool while he gave me script notes, enthroned in one of those giant leather vibrating Sharper Image chairs.”
CBS casting head Peter Golden was vehemently against casting Jon Cryer in “Two and a Half Men.” “I asked why. I was told … he was the death of comedy,” he writes. But Cryer nailed it, and Moonves reluctantly gave in: “I’m going to give you enough rope.”
When Warner Bros. and CBS looked to bring up “The Big Bang Theory” episodic fees for Mayim Bialik and Melissa Rauch, the show’s original five stars (Jim Parsons, Kaley Cuoco, Johnny Galecki, Simon Helberg and Kunal Nayyar) were asked to take a 10% pay cut to accommodate those raises. “I assumed they’d quickly agree, you know, all for one, one for all. Wrong again. They were outraged that they would even be asked to take a small cut in order to reward the two newer cast members.” But, he added, “despite becoming insanely wealthy and famous on a global scale, most everyone in the cast of ‘The Big Bang Theory’ is filled with gratitude. Only a few don’t take my calls.”
CBS also pushed back on casting Melissa McCarthy in “Mike & Molly.” “Believe it or not, they wanted a hot young woman to play a woman struggling with her weight. It was even suggested by one exec — a female exec — that I consider casting a more attractive actress and put her in a fat suit.”
Lorre was reluctant to hire Anna Faris for “Mom,” and writes that “as the years went by, it became apparent that my initial reluctance to hire Anna was, in fact, correct. After six years, she left the show for mysterious reasons that were not mysterious to anyone on the show.”
Before Michael Douglas was cast as the star of “The Kominsky Method,” Lorre held a table read with Al Pacino in the main role. It didn’t go well. “He was all over the place, improvising dialogue, losing his place in the script, throwing off all the other actors … Afterward, Mr. Pacino told me the only way he could do this was if he improvised his dialogue. I finally sprouted a pair of balls and said, ‘No fucking way!’”
Lorre has a new theory on what may have led to Charlie Sheen’s meltdown on “Two and a Half Men.” When it appeared on set that Sheen was struggling, Lorre cut the season early — and two episodes short. “Here’s the guess: In my wildest dreams, I never considered that Charlie might have needed the money that two more episodes would’ve paid.” He theorizes that Sheen may have lost some serious money on sports bets, and perhaps needed the money to settle a debt with some bad people.



	Lorre spoke to Variety about “Sitcom.” Here’s that chat, condensed for clarity and length:
	
		What made you decide to share some really personal stuff?	

	I decided if I’m going to do this, I’m going to tell the truth as best I can. That includes the truth about my — let’s be gracious and call them missteps, but blunders could also be a word. There was no point in doing it if I was going to sugarcoat my life.
	
	
		Your decade in Scientology was a surprise. Why have you never discussed that before?	

	It was embarrassing to me that I burned a decade of my life up in that thing. Seriously, 10 years of living in this artificial bubble. I can wallow in regret or I can choose to recognize that even that was a step that had to be taken to get to where I am.
	
		At the time in the ’70s, you signed a billion-year contract with Scientology. Is that still enforceable?	

	If there’s a knock at the door, I’ll let you know. That’s very funny. As I was writing that, I’m going, ‘am I making myself liable here?’
	
		When you cast Jenna Elfman in “Dharma & Greg,” you downplayed the fact that you had left the church.	

	In my effort to try and get ‘Dharma and Greg’ to actually become a reality, I downplayed the fact that I’d run for the exits — so as not to polarize myself with Jenna, because she was deeply enmeshed in it with her husband. Yet I truly understood her worldview because I had lived it. I remember saying to the writers, I wasn’t going to tolerate making fun of her for her beliefs. She was a joyful, happy, productive part of that ensemble, and given the journey I’d been on with Roseanne and Brett Butler and Cybil Shepard, Jenna was a delight. I thought it was really important to disregard her personal beliefs. Of course I probably was hiding the fact because of my very insecure attitude about my own involvement in that organization. A year to two later, after the show was over, when I approached her with the idea for a series called “Three Cinderellas,” that’s when apparently her mind had been changing about me.
	
		You call out Carsey-Werner for being absentee producers as their stars were behaving badly.	

	You can understand it from a purely business economic perspective. The business model was produce 100 episodes of a network situation comedy, and then go sell it into syndication reruns, and become wealthy. It was almost a guarantee that 100 episodes equals wealth, and a windfall of income for many years to come. That was the principle I think that was at work there: Ignore the misbehavior of the stars, and do everything you can to keep it going and get to that magic number of 100 episodes. With that as an economic model, morality and fair play was nonsense. [Carsey-Werner did not respond to a request for comment.]
	
		Your theory that the 2007 WGA strike, which helped elevate “The Apprentice,” helped bring about the end of democracy might have some legs.	

	I think that needs to be discussed. That the Writers Guild has to take responsibility for the end of the Western world. I’m allowed to have whatever ridiculous hypotheses I want to have.
	
	
		You were surprised that the “Big Bang Theory” stars wouldn’t take a pay cut so the newer cast could get a raise.	

	No one involved in the show was prepared for that enormous success and the financial results. And yeah, I remember being disappointed that there wasn’t a “one for all, all for one” attitude. But when you’re talking to someone in that position and they’ve suddenly gone from a Toyota Tercel to a Mercedes limo, it’s an extraordinary transition for anybody. People’s responses were also colored by everyone suddenly having lawyers and managers and agents, wives, husbands, boyfriends, girlfriends, friends. Everybody. There was a collective response to that, and incredibly disorienting for all of us. Nobody was equipped for that kind of that kind of skyrocket that the show became.
	
		You say only a few of them don’t return your calls. Do we play the guessing game now?	

	By all means, go ahead and guess. But we are not going to have that conversation.
	
		You have a theory that Charlie Sheen melted down because the episodic order for “Two and a Half Men” had been trimmed, but he needed the money.	

	It’s important to point out: I don’t know that for a fact. As I said in the book, this was a theory I had way in the rearview mirror, looking backward that might have been what was going on. It’s never been discussed. I could be entirely wrong, but nothing else makes sense. It was a really dark, turbulent, frightening, angry time. A couple of years, really. It was hard to make sense of it all when it was happening. It was hard to make sense of it all when it was happening. I hope what comes through in the book is, at the end of the day, we reconciled [on Lorre’s show ‘Bookie’]. It was an enormously gratifying experience working with him again, even to the point where I reached out to him and said, “How would you feel about writing the blurb for this book I wrote?” And you look at look at the back of the book, one of the funniest things is Charlie’s blurb.
	
		At the end of the book you say, even the things that you regret, they happened, and you wound up where you are today.	

	It is a treatise in regret. I don’t know that I understood this when I started writing this thing, but I think I have some perspective on it now. Regret, while a very human attitude, is an attempt to rewrite the past, right? Or at least swim in it. But my story is such that the things I would normally regret — they were what led me to a career and a life I could never have dreamed of, way beyond my dreams. So, how much do I want to indulge myself in regret?
	
	
		In Chapter 24, you recount the many owners Warner Bros. has had while you’ve worked there. What do you make of the recent merger under Skydance?	

	None of that touches what I do for a living, which is to try to make people laugh. That’s my job. That’s why they pay me the crazy money. That’s what I do when I go to Burbank. And the corporate superstructure, whether it’s AOL, Time Warner, AT&T, Discovery, now Paramount — it really has very little to do with the work on the ground.
	
		But there was always the business tension of CBS and Warner Bros. pushing for the best deal for your shows. Now that the studio and network are under the same roof, do you worry about self-dealing?	

	There was always that clash of the two corporations. That clash, I guess, now is gone. But what difference does it make? So is network television.
	
		Do you have concerns that consolidation will lead to fewer opportunities for writers?	

	I’m kind of a naive optimist. I see this environment as incredibly exciting and vibrant. There’s so many opportunities, platforms where you can go and say, “Here’s an idea for a show. Give me money so I can make it.” I couldn’t have gone to CBS with “The Kominsky Method.” That’s a universe that was driven, and perhaps still is driven by demographics. They’re not going to do a show about 75- and 80-year-old men wrestling with the minutiae of growing old. I mention in the book, HBO and Hulu and Amazon and Apple all passed on it. But Ted Sarandos and Netflix said yes, and I got to make something that was really a deeply felt and personal project. I know it’s a cliche, but it was indeed a labor of love.
	
		The one thing that you don’t mention in the book is all your philanthropy.	

	I didn’t want it to be in the book. That’s just self-aggrandizement. That’s not the point of doing that stuff. The point of doing that stuff is trying to make a difference, and not to pound your chest and go “look at me, look what I did.”
	
		Are you bracing for anyone to call you after they read your book?	

	It’s certainly something I actually had to think about. But again, as I said somewhere in there, this is my memory of how things went down. And if you disagree, write your own fucking book.

            Six Flags hasn’t just taken a massive blow to their reputation … their stocks got hit hard after a parkgoer tragically died at their Georgia location.
      
    
            According to Forbes, Six Flags’ stock prices had significantly dropped when the market opened on Tuesday to the lowest level since 2009.
      
    
            The outlet reports prices had dipped under $10 per share at one point … and were still down more than 14% just before the market was closed for the day.
      

      
        
              
    
    
            The drop comes after Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was killed after being ejected from the Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            9 roller coasters across 6 of the company's theme parks were shut down after Hassan’s tragic death and the investigation is ongoing.

title: Kelly Clarkson’s Art of Play Visit Caught on Newly Released Security Footage
description:
Kelly Clarkson
                          Seen at Art of Play in Newly Released Security Footage
body:
Kelly Clarkson
                          Seen at Art of Play in Newly Released Security Footage
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 13, 2026
                            7:01 PM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Kelly Clarkson's battle with a Brooklyn curiosity shop over a $15,000 singing bird named Molly may have a new piece of evidence in the mix ... security footage from her visit to the store.
      
    
            In the video, obtained by Pablo Torres, it captures the day Kelly stopped by the store to inquire about the mechanical bird that's now at the center of a full-blown online feud.
      
    
            You can see Kelly enter the store and begin picking up various items ... before approaching the $15,000 bird in question, "Molly." She's then seen talking to an employee and pointing to Molly on the wall -- unfortunately the footage has no audio.
      

            About 5 minutes after she entered, Kelly is seen waving her hands and emotionally talking to the worker at the entrance, before she's seen exiting the shop for good.
      
    
            As we previously reported ... Kelly first took the dispute public over the weekend, claiming she drove to Art of Play intending to buy several items, only to feel like an employee assumed she couldn't afford what she wanted.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The singer compared the experience to Julia Roberts getting snubbed in the legendary film "Pretty Woman" ... and warned the shop it had just lost a major sale.
      
    
            Art of Play initially claimed Molly was a one-of-a-kind singing and dancing automaton permanently attached to the wall and not for sale. Kelly fired back, accusing the shop of lying and insisting an employee pointed to a $15,000 price tag before offering to find her something comparable.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The store later clarified its position, saying the $15,000 price was for a nearly identical bird owned by Seattle artist Bliss Kolb. It also claimed staff offered to show Kelly a different singing bird available for around $2,000 ... but she left before ever seeing it.
      
    
            Now, the security footage adds another layer to the increasingly messy dispute ... however, surveillance footage may document the visit visually, but it can't necessarily settle a disagreement over tone or exactly how a conversation went down.
      
    
            The online fallout has been massive, with supporters of both sides weighing in and the small business facing a wave of public scrutiny. The controversy has also sparked debate over whether a celebrity's social media callout is fair game when a local business disputes the account.
      
    
            As for whether the newly released footage backs Kelly's account, the store's version, or neither completely ... that's up to the jury of the internet to decide.

schema.headline: Kelly Clarkson’s Art of Play Visit Caught on Newly Released Security Footage
